title: The Second Greater Element

concept.title: Two stacks: waiting for the first greater, waiting for the second
body: For every element, the **second greater element** is the second element to its right (in order of position) that is strictly greater than it. The next greater element needs one stack of elements waiting for their first greater element. Here an element waits **twice**: first for the first greater element, then for the second. Use two stacks: `first` (waiting for the first greater) and `second` (already seen one greater element, waiting for the second).

When a new element `x = a[i]` arrives: (1) every element on the **`second`** stack that is smaller than `x` has now found its second greater element: its answer is `x`. (2) Every element on the **`first`** stack that is smaller than `x` has found its first greater element: it moves to the **`second`** stack. (3) Push `i` on `first`. The order matters: step (1) must come before step (2), otherwise the element would find its first and second greater element in the same moment.

The moved elements are put on the second stack in their original order. Then both stacks stay sorted (non-increasing from the bottom to the top), so the elements to be settled are always on top. Every index is moved at most twice: O(n).

statement: For each element of an array, find its second greater element: looking to the right, the second element (in order of position) that is strictly greater than it. Print its value for every element, or -1 if there is no such element.

examples.note: For 2 the greater elements to the right are 4 and 9: the second is 9. For 4 they are 9 and 6: the second is 6. For 0 they are 9 and 6: 6. The last two have none. Answer: 9 6 6 -1 -1.

hints: One stack gives the first greater element. Use a second stack for the elements that have already seen one.
Process the second stack first, then move elements from the first stack to the second.
Keep the moved elements in the same order, so that the second stack stays monotonic.

explanation: The first stack holds elements waiting for their first greater element, the second one elements waiting for the second. A new element settles the second stack, then moves the smaller elements of the first stack to the second, keeping their order.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

res = [-1] * n
first = []
second = []
for i in range(n):
    while second and a[second[-1]] < a[i]:
        res[second.pop()] = a[i]
    moved = []
    while first and a[first[-1]] < a[i]:
        moved.append(first.pop())
    second.extend(reversed(moved))
    first.append(i)
print(*res)
